risk_assessment.rationale: The combination of a successful logon from an unrecognized source with a high volume of scanning patterns raises concern that the account may have been compromised or is being used for malicious reconnaissance. Because the IP has no known provider information and there is no direct evidence of further attack, the risk is considered medium—enough to warrant immediate containment steps but not yet definitive proof of compromise.

recommended_actions_freeform_experimenta: Immediately isolate the affected workstation or virtual machine from the internal network to prevent lateral movement while investigation proceeds.
Force a password reset for user *mrahman* and enforce MFA if not already in place; consider disabling the account temporarily until the compromise can be ruled out.

Collect volatile memory, disk images, and system logs (including Security Event Log, Sysmon, and Windows Defender ATP) from the host that logged the successful authentication to look for signs of credential theft or persistence mechanisms.
Run a full endpoint scan with an up‑to‑date antivirus/EDR solution and check for known malicious binaries or suspicious scheduled tasks that may have been installed during the scanning activity.

Perform a network flow analysis (NetFlow, sFlow) around the time of the login to identify any outbound connections from the host to external IPs other than 100.72.44.19, which could indicate data exfiltration or command‑and‑control traffic.
Cross‑reference the 42 scanning events with threat intelligence feeds; if any of those patterns match known adversary behaviors (e.g., port scans, SMB enumeration), prioritize further investigation.
If possible, correlate the login event with other security tools (SIEM, IDS/IPS) to see whether there were any alerts for anomalous activity on that host or network segment.
Document all findings and maintain a timeline of events; this will aid in determining whether the account was legitimately used by an authorized user or compromised.
